description: Figure 3, the top group of pie charts, displays the problem distribution based on correctness under with-knowledge (w/ knowledge) and without-knowledge (w/o knowledge) settings, using the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting method. This group consists of three pie charts, one for each difficulty level: “easy,” “medium,” and “hard.” Each chart is divided into four colored segments representing different combinations of correctness in the two settings: teal for N+K+ (correct in both), yellow for N−K+ (incorrect without knowledge, correct with knowledge), orange for N−K− (incorrect in both), and red for N+K− (correct without knowledge, incorrect with knowledge). For the “easy” problems, the distribution is 40.6% N+K+, 45.9% N−K+, 10.1% N−K−, and 3.3% N+K−. For “medium” problems, it is 44.6% N+K+, 44.3% N−K+, 7.2% N−K−, and 3.9% N+K−. For “hard” problems, the distribution is 36.2% N+K+, 36.8% N−K+, 20.1% N−K−, and 7.0% N+K−. A legend to the right of the charts identifies the color coding for each category. The caption notes that easier problems are mainly hindered by a lack of knowledge, while the bottleneck for hard problems lies in geometric knowledge reasoning abilities.
